title: NIH Grant Awards and Funding Opportunity Notices Fell, Analysts Say
date_basis: March 15, 2026 is the dated snapshot for Ginexi's notice analysis; VPM separately reports Berg's early-2026 award count.
description_short: Analysts report fewer NIH grants and delayed funding notices; the counts measure different things.
description_medium: An NPR report quoted Jeremy Berg’s analysis that NIH had issued about 2,300 new grants in early 2026, roughly 66% fewer than in the comparable period a year earlier. It also reported Elizabeth Ginexi’s finding that 205 of 336 open forecasts were past their promised posting dates. Separately, Ginexi’s Chronicle analysis counted 756 funding-opportunity notices in 2024, 120 in 2025 and 14 by March 15, 2026. Awards and notices are different measures; these attributed counts do not establish covert intent or a shift to larger grants.
description_long: A May 2026 NPR report carried by VPM quoted former NIH official Jeremy Berg’s analysis that the National Institutes of Health had issued roughly 2,300 new grants in the first few months of 2026, about 66% fewer than in the comparable period a year earlier. The report also quoted former NIH program officer Elizabeth Ginexi, whose review found that 205 of 336 NIH funding forecasts still listed as open were past their promised posting dates without a full announcement. Separately, Ginexi’s Chronicle of Higher Education analysis counted 756 NIH funding-opportunity notices posted in 2024, 120 in 2025 and 14 by March 15, 2026; she said 61 of 75 notices forecast for 2026 had not yet been published. These figures describe distinct measures: grants issued, delayed forecasts and posted notices. They document a sharp slowdown and delays as reported by named analysts, but do not prove that NIH acted covertly, deliberately shifted to larger awards, or concealed an intact budget. VPM also reports the administration’s explanation for funding delays; that explanation does not resolve the cause of each count. The original headline’s claim of covert manipulation is unsupported.

sources.title: VPM/NPR, Researchers say the Trump administration is finding new ways to punish science
sources.supports: Reports Berg's roughly 2,300 NIH awards and 66% year-over-year decline in the first months of 2026; attributes Ginexi's finding that 205 of 336 open forecasts were overdue; includes HHS's stated explanation for delays.

sources.title: The Chronicle of Higher Education, Why Is the NIH Abandoning Science?
sources.supports: Ginexi's Grants.gov analysis of NIH funding-opportunity notices: 756 in 2024, 120 in 2025, 14 by March 15, 2026, and 61 of 75 forecast 2026 notices not yet published.

notes: The prior draft conflated grants awarded with funding-opportunity notices and overstated intent. Keep the separate VPM/NPR and Chronicle counts attributed to their analysts; source_triage was needs_correction, not accepted_source.

title: FEC Lacks a Voting Quorum as Enforcement Backlog Reaches at Least 195 Matters
date_basis: The reviewed sources do not establish the precise date the Commission first fell below quorum; the exact start date remains unresolved.
description_short: FEC quorum loss limited commission votes; NOTUS reported at least 195 pending enforcement matters in March 2026.
description_medium: Ellen Weintraub disputed Trump’s January 2025 attempt to remove her from the FEC. After later commissioner departures, the Commission lacked the four affirmative votes required for certain actions. NOTUS reported at least 195 pending enforcement matters in early March 2026, citing Chair Shana Broussard. The reports support a voting and enforcement backlog, not the claim that the FEC could take no action of any kind or lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump’s term; the exact onset is not established here.
description_long: President Donald Trump sent Federal Election Commission Chair Ellen Weintraub a letter purporting to remove her in January 2025; she disputed the legality of the move. Subsequent commissioner departures left the Commission without the four affirmative votes required for certain commission actions. The FEC’s announcement about Commissioner Allen Dickerson’s departure documents a later vacancy, while NOTUS reported in early March 2026 that at least 195 enforcement matters were pending, citing Chair Shana Broussard. Those facts support a serious constraint on commission-level enforcement decisions and a reported backlog. They do not establish that the agency could take no action of any kind, that every pending matter was caused by the quorum loss, or that the Commission lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of the president’s term. The cited material does not give a sufficiently documented start date for the period without quorum, so this correction leaves the precise date unresolved rather than repeating May 1, 2025 as settled. It also does not establish a zero-dollar fine total or the timing of later nominations. The entry is limited to the disputed removal, later vacancies, and reported March 2026 backlog.

sources.title: Reuters, U.S. FEC commissioner-chair says Trump removed her from office
sources.supports: Reports Weintraub's disputed removal and the four-vote threshold for Commission action.

sources.title: Federal Election Commission, Commissioner Allen J. Dickerson announces departure
sources.supports: Official notice of Dickerson's departure and Commission meeting actions that failed to receive four affirmative votes.

sources.title: NOTUS, Trump Put the FEC on Ice; Its Return Remains an Open Question
sources.supports: Reports the Commission's loss of quorum and the resulting limits on commission action.

sources.title: NOTUS, The FEC’s Investigation Backlog is Growing — With No End in Sight
sources.supports: Reports at least 195 pending enforcement matters in early March 2026, citing the FEC chair.

notes: Precise no-quorum start date, duration percentage and fine total remain unsupported by the reviewed sources; do not present them as verified.

title: Social Security Administration Announces Plan to Reduce Workforce from About 57,000 to 50,000
description_short: SSA set a 50,000-employee target, down from about 57,000, while anticipating many voluntary departures.
description_medium: On February 28, 2025, the Social Security Administration announced a target to reduce staffing from roughly 57,000 employees to 50,000 while reorganizing its regional and headquarters structure. SSA said it expected many departures through retirement, deferred resignation and voluntary separation, while leaving open possible reductions in force. The release states a workforce plan; it does not show that thousands had already been involuntarily fired or establish later service effects.
description_long: On February 28, 2025, the Social Security Administration announced a plan to reduce its workforce from roughly 57,000 employees to 50,000 and reorganize its regional and headquarters structure. The stated target was a reduction of about 7,000 positions. SSA said it expected much of the reduction to come through retirement, deferred resignation and voluntary separation incentives, while also allowing that reductions in force could be used. The agency’s release described a workforce target and planned changes; it did not say that DOGE itself ordered or carried out thousands of involuntary terminations. A staffing target and an expectation of voluntary departures do not establish how many employees ultimately left, how many positions were eliminated through layoffs, or what happened to local service capacity. Those outcomes require later agency records or independent reporting. The original July 2025 headline also misdates the announcement: the cited SSA release is dated February 28. This entry therefore reports the announced target and the agency’s stated approach without presenting proposed reductions as completed firings or asserting unmeasured operational consequences.

sources.title: Social Security Administration, Social Security Administration Announces Agency Restructuring
sources.supports: Official February 28, 2025 announcement of the approximate 57,000-to-50,000 staffing target and expected use of retirement and voluntary separation, with possible RIF actions.

notes: The cited release documents an announced target, not completed layoffs or a measured service impact.

title: Trump Removes NLRB Member and Two EEOC Commissioners, Leaving Both Bodies Without Quorums
description_short: Trump removed one NLRB member and two EEOC commissioners; both agencies lost a quorum for certain board-level decisions.
description_medium: On January 27, 2025, President Trump removed NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox and EEOC commissioners Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels. Reuters reported that vacancies left both bodies without a quorum for specified board- or commission-level decisions. The reports document a constraint on formal board action, not the firing of every member or the end of every agency function; they do not establish that all investigations or regional enforcement stopped.
description_long: On January 27, 2025, President Donald Trump removed National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission commissioners Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels. Reuters reported that existing vacancies combined with these removals left both agencies without the quorum needed for specified board- or commission-level decisions. The NLRB’s official biography confirms that Wilcox’s term was due to end in 2028 and says Trump removed her before its expiration. The two agencies have different responsibilities: the NLRB handles labor relations and unfair labor practice matters, while the EEOC addresses employment discrimination. Losing a quorum constrained formal collective decisions, but the cited reports do not show that every member was fired, that every investigation stopped, or that regional enforcement work ceased. Legal challenges over the removals followed. This narrower account corrects the original claim that Trump fired all members and paralyzed both agencies, while retaining the documented institutional consequence: each body lacked a quorum for actions requiring a vote of the full board or commission.

sources.title: Reuters, Trump fires U.S. labor board member, hobbling agency amid legal battles
sources.supports: Reports Wilcox's January 27 removal and its effect on the NLRB's quorum and decision-making.

sources.title: Reuters, Trump hobbles U.S. anti-discrimination agency by firing Democrats
sources.supports: Reports the removal of EEOC commissioners Burrows and Samuels and the resulting loss of a commission quorum.

sources.title: National Labor Relations Board, Gwynne A. Wilcox
sources.supports: Officially records Wilcox's term through August 27, 2028 and her January 27, 2025 removal.

notes: Corrected the date and scope; the supplied evidence supports quorum loss, not a total shutdown of all agency work.

title: DOGE Sought IRS Data Access; Officials Agreed to Limit Access to Anonymized Data
description_short: Reports say DOGE sought IRS data access, then agreed to read-only access to anonymized data rather than individual returns.
description_medium: In February 2025, DOGE personnel sought access to IRS systems during the administration’s government-wide review. The Washington Post reported that Treasury and White House officials later agreed to limit the IRS DOGE representative to read-only, anonymized data and bar access to personal taxpayer information. These reports document an access request and negotiated restrictions; they do not show that DOGE inspected tax returns belonging to political opponents, donors or journalists.
description_long: In February 2025, Department of Government Efficiency personnel sought access to sensitive Internal Revenue Service systems as part of the administration’s government-wide review. The Washington Post reported the initial request on February 16 and, four days later, reported an agreement by Treasury and White House officials to prohibit access to personal taxpayer data and limit the DOGE representative’s access to read-only, anonymized data. That sequence matters: the request raised legitimate concerns because tax records contain highly sensitive personal and financial information, but a request followed by a negotiated access limit is not evidence that DOGE inspected identifiable returns. The supplied reports do not document DOGE viewing individual returns belonging to political opponents, donors or journalists. The supported account concerns the proposed access, privacy safeguards and questions about oversight, not a demonstrated political search of taxpayer files. Any claim about data actually queried or safeguards breached would require separate records showing what information was available and how it was used. This correction keeps the reported access dispute while removing the unsupported claim that DOGE accessed political opponents’ tax records.

sources.title: The Washington Post, DOGE seeks access to IRS taxpayer data
sources.supports: Reports DOGE's request for access to IRS systems and taxpayer data as part of a government-wide review.

title: Trump Says He Knows More About Renewables Than ‘Any Human Being on Earth’
description_short: In a 2016 interview, Trump boasted about renewables knowledge and criticized solar’s payback period.
description_medium: During an April 13, 2016 Hannity interview, Donald Trump said he knew more about renewables than “any human being on earth.” He then said he liked solar but criticized its payback period and power output. The transcript supports a 2016 boast about renewables generally, not a 2020 claim of unmatched solar expertise; it does not verify his technical assertions.
description_long: On April 13, 2016, during an interview with Sean Hannity, then-presidential candidate Donald Trump discussed energy policy and said he knew more about renewables than “any human being on earth.” He followed the boast by saying he liked solar, then criticizing what he described as a 30-year payback period and limited power output; he also referred to a 32-year estimate raised in the exchange. The transcript records Trump’s words and his stated view of solar economics. It does not establish his comparative expertise or test the technical accuracy of his payback claims, which depend on factors such as system cost, financing and location that the interview did not examine. The original entry misdated the remark as a 2020 solar-specific claim. The correction places it in the 2016 campaign and describes the wording accurately as a claim about renewables overall, followed by comments about solar. This record documents campaign rhetoric, not an independent assessment of renewable-energy economics.

sources.title: Fox News, Trump explains why he feels the primary process is ‘unfair’
sources.supports: Transcript of the April 13, 2016 Hannity interview, including Trump's exact renewables boast and his comments on solar payback and power.

notes: The transcript supports the quote and date, not the claim that Trump had unmatched expertise or that his payback estimate was technically accurate.

title: Reuters Describes Stephen Miller as a Central Driver of Trump’s Immigration Agenda
description_short: Reuters describes Stephen Miller as a central driver of the administration’s immigration agenda, not its sole author.
description_medium: A July 11, 2025 Reuters profile described White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller as a central figure driving President Trump’s aggressive immigration agenda. The reporting supports a claim about Miller’s influence, but does not establish that he personally drafted every executive order, legal theory or enforcement procedure associated with the administration’s policies.
description_long: A Reuters profile published July 11, 2025, described White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller as a central figure driving and championing President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration agenda. The account supports a description of Miller as an influential policy driver in the administration. It does not establish that he alone designed or drafted every executive order, legal theory, enforcement procedure or operational decision associated with the immigration campaign. Those policies involved multiple officials, agencies and legal processes, so comprehensive personal attribution would require evidence tied to each action. This corrected entry focuses on the role that the cited reporting documents: Miller’s significant influence over the administration’s direction. It does not claim sole authorship or use the profile alone to quantify deportations, establish due-process findings, or prove the effects of particular policies. Those questions require separate evidence. The original entry’s broad account of Miller as architect of every element of the legal framework goes beyond the cited source; the narrower, attributed description preserves the documented significance of his role without overstating what Reuters reported.

sources.title: Reuters, White House aide driving Trump’s aggressive immigration agenda
sources.supports: July 11, 2025 profile describing Miller's central role and influence in shaping and driving the administration's immigration agenda.

notes: The source supports central influence, not sole authorship of every order, legal theory or operation.

title: Agencies Pause Enforcement of New 2024 Mental Health Parity Rule Provisions
description_short: Agencies paused enforcement of new 2024 parity-rule provisions; MHPAEA’s statutory duties and 2013 rule remained in effect.
description_medium: On May 15, 2025, the Departments of Labor, HHS and Treasury said they would not enforce requirements newly added by the 2024 Mental Health Parity final rule while related litigation proceeded and for 18 months after a final decision. The agencies said MHPAEA’s statutory obligations and the 2013 rule remained in effect. This was a limited enforcement pause, not a repeal of parity law or an end to all enforcement.
description_long: On May 15, 2025, the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and the Treasury announced that they would not enforce provisions newly added by the 2024 final rule implementing the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA) while related litigation was pending and for 18 months after a final decision. The agencies explicitly said that MHPAEA’s statutory requirements and the earlier 2013 rule remained in effect. The announcement therefore changed the enforcement status of newer requirements; it did not repeal the parity statute, end every parity obligation or make insurers free of all requirements. The original entry gives the wrong date and overstates the action as an end to parity enforcement. The agencies’ statement does not establish that insurers then changed specific coverage practices, narrowed particular networks or denied treatment to a stated number of people. Those effects would need separate evidence. The supported correction is limited to the scope and timing of the announced pause and the obligations the agencies said continued to apply; the source does not establish the later outcome of litigation or reconsideration.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Labor, Statement Regarding Enforcement of the Final Rule on Requirements Related to MHPAEA
sources.supports: May 15, 2025 joint-agency statement describing the limited pause for new 2024-rule provisions and confirming statutory MHPAEA obligations and the 2013 rule remained in effect.

notes: Does not infer that insurers changed coverage or that the parity statute was suspended.

title: Trump Removes NLRB Member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo
description_short: Trump removed NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo on January 27, 2025.
description_medium: On January 27, 2025, President Trump removed NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo. Reuters reported that Wilcox’s removal left the five-member Board without a quorum and unable to issue decisions. Abruzzo was the agency’s general counsel, not a Board member. The reporting does not support the claim that Trump fired every Board member or that all NLRB functions stopped.
description_long: On January 27, 2025, President Donald Trump removed National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo. Reuters reported that Wilcox’s removal deprived the five-member Board of a quorum, preventing it from issuing decisions. The NLRB had two other vacancies, so removing Wilcox affected the Board’s ability to act; Abruzzo held the separate role of general counsel and was not another Board member. The agency said no reason was given for the dismissals, and Wilcox challenged her removal in court. This was a consequential intervention in NLRB leadership, but it did not remove every sitting Board member. The supplied reporting supports a limit on Board decisions while it lacked a quorum, not the claim that all agency functions disappeared or that every pending labor case was frozen indefinitely. This corrected entry replaces the original January 20 date and blanket shutdown description with the specific removals and quorum consequence reported at the time. Later litigation and staffing developments are separate events and are not inferred here.

sources.title: Reuters, Trump fires U.S. labor board member, hobbling agency amid legal battles
sources.supports: Reports the January 27 removals of Wilcox and Abruzzo and the effect of Wilcox's departure on the NLRB quorum and decisions.

sources.title: Reuters, Former NLRB member sues Trump administration over firing
sources.supports: Reports Wilcox's legal challenge to her removal and the dispute over the president's authority.

notes: Wilcox was the Board member; Abruzzo was General Counsel. The supported consequence is loss of quorum for Board decisions, not a total agency shutdown.

title: Reporting Describes DOGE Access to Sensitive HHS Systems and a Child-Support Database
description_short: Reports describe DOGE access to sensitive HHS systems and child-support data, not unrestricted access to complete medical records.
description_medium: Reporting based on HHS court filings said DOGE affiliates had access to 19 sensitive HHS systems; WIRED noted one instance apparently lacked required security training. The Washington Post separately reported read-only access to a child-support database containing income information. These reports raise access and privacy concerns but do not establish unrestricted access to millions of people’s complete medical records, diagnoses or prescriptions.
description_long: In March and April 2025, reporting described DOGE affiliates’ access to sensitive systems at the Department of Health and Human Services. WIRED, citing court filings and depositions, reported access to 19 systems, including financial and program databases, and said one affiliate apparently lacked required security training for a particularly sensitive system. The Washington Post separately reported that DOGE associates received read-only access to a child-support database containing income information, despite objections from career employees. Together, these reports document access to multiple government systems and raise questions about safeguards. They do not establish that DOGE had unrestricted access to complete medical records for millions of Americans, including HIV status, mental-health diagnoses or prescription histories. Nor do they show that every affiliate saw every record, that access was universally unauthorized, or that data was misused. Those stronger claims would require records identifying the systems and fields available to particular users, evidence about authorization and audit controls, and proof of actual access. This correction reports the scope the articles describe and preserves the evidence gap around detailed clinical records rather than repeating the original claim of carte-blanche access.

sources.title: WIRED, Here’s All the Health and Human Services Data DOGE Has Access To
sources.supports: Reports, citing court filings and depositions, DOGE affiliates' access to 19 HHS systems and an apparent instance of missing required security training.

sources.title: The Washington Post, HHS gives DOGE access to sensitive child-support database
sources.supports: Reports read-only access to a child-support database containing income information and objections by career employees.

notes: The sources do not substantiate complete clinical records, named diagnoses or prescriptions, universal authorization failures, or carte-blanche access; retain that evidence gap explicitly.
